mechanisms.kill: The antioxidant that keeps your cells from going rancid
mechanisms.figure_alt: A fatty cell membrane: intact on the left, guarded at its centre by selenium, gone rancid with a visible age spot on the right.

beats.title: Your cells are fat
beats.text: Every cell and every mitochondrion is wrapped in a membrane made of fat — and fat oxidizes, goes rancid, the same way cooking oil does once it's heated or left out.
beats.hook: The rancidity that spoils oil in the pan can happen inside your own cell walls.

beats.title: The most efficient antioxidant
beats.text: Selenium — working through the glutathione-peroxidase enzyme system — is, in Wallach's telling, the most efficient antioxidant there is, standing guard over those fatty membranes right at the subcellular level.
beats.hook: A trace mineral you need in millionths of a gram is the bodyguard on every membrane you own.

beats.title: Rancid, made visible
beats.text: Pull selenium out and the fats peroxidize — the brown-gold residue (ceroid lipofuscin) surfaces on skin as "age spots" or "liver spots," while selenium-starved heart muscle can fail outright, as in Keshan disease and the sudden collapse of young athletes.
beats.hook: An age spot is rancid fat you can see — Wallach reads it as a warning, not a blemish.

mechanisms.kill: The same shortage shows up in your mirror and in your arteries.
mechanisms.figure_alt: Copper feeds two enzymes. Tyrosinase makes hair pigment: black, brown, auburn or blond hair all turn white or grey when copper runs short — the first visible sign. Lysyl oxidase makes the elastin in artery walls, and without it the wall balloons into an aneurysm.

left.head: The one you can see
left.text: Copper is the cofactor for tyrosinase — the enzyme that works on tyrosine to make the melanin that colours hair. Whatever your natural colour, short the copper and the pigment stops being made: it grows back white, grey or silver.

right.head: The one you can’t
right.text: Copper is also the cofactor for lysyl oxidase — the enzyme that converts pro-elastin into the elastin that gives an artery wall its tensile strength. Short the copper and the wall gives where the pressure is highest.

mechanisms.bridge: They don’t arrive together — and that is the whole point. The visible one runs decades ahead of the silent one, which is what makes grey hair worth reading rather than covering up.

figure_pre_beats.alt: A timeline: pigment goes first, then structure, then the artery wall, ending in rupture — decades of warning.

beats.title: Pigment goes
beats.text: Tyrosinase needs copper to make melanin. Pigment is the first thing to fail — and the first thing you can see.

beats.title: Structure goes
beats.text: The same shortage, further along. Elastin thins: skin wrinkles deeply, spider and varicose veins surface, and artery walls lose the tensile strength that keeps them from ballooning.

beats.title: Copper restores it
beats.text: Wallach reports the sequence running in reverse on plant-derived colloidal copper — original hair colour returning, veins receding, and some aneurysms healing.

figure_post_beats.alt: A return track in blue running right to left across the same span: add plant-derived colloidal copper, and normal hair colour returns in six months.
